question: Alina writes the numbers \(1,\) \(2,\) \(\cdots,\) \(9\) on separate cards, one number per card. She wishes to divide the cards into \(3\) groups of \(3\) cards so that the sum of the numbers in each group will be the same. In how many ways can this be done?
solution:
The cards total \(1+2+\cdots+9=45\), so each of the three groups must sum to \(15\). Because \(15\) is odd, each group must contain either one or three odd cards. There are five odd cards in all, so the only possible distribution is \(3,1,1\): exactly one group contains three odd cards.

Find that group first. If its smallest card is \(1\), the other two odd cards must sum to \(14\), giving \(5,9\). If its smallest card is \(3\), the other two must sum to \(12\), giving \(5,7\). A smallest card of at least \(5\) would make the sum at least \(5+7+9=21\). Thus the three-odd-card group is either \(\{1,5,9\}\) or \(\{3,5,7\}\).

If it is \(\{1,5,9\}\), the remaining odd cards are \(3\) and \(7\). The card \(3\) needs two even cards totaling \(12\); from \(2,4,6,8\), only \(4+8\) works. The last group is then \(\{2,6,7\}\), which also sums to \(15\).

If it is \(\{3,5,7\}\), the remaining odd cards are \(1\) and \(9\). The card \(1\) needs two even cards totaling \(14\), forcing \(6+8\). The last group is \(\{2,4,9\}\), again summing to \(15\).

Each case gives one division, and every valid division has exactly one three-odd-card group, so none has been omitted or counted twice. There are \(\boxed{2}\) ways, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
